title: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
summary: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory Project page: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

AI.tldr: To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layou...

title: ADEPT: Adaptive Monocular Depth Estimation via Model-In-The-Loop Photometric Tuning with Capture Risk Prediction
summary: ADEPT: Adaptive Monocular Depth Estimation via Model-In-The-Loop Photometric Tuning with Capture Risk Prediction Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.

AI.tldr: We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model.

title: GenPA: Image Generators as Efficient Robot Policies
summary: GenPA: Image Generators as Efficient Robot Policies Project page: Pretrained visual generation models have shown great promise in robotic manipulation. However, a representative line of work still treats future visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes are no longer generated at inference time. We argue that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their combinations within a common policy architecture. At deployment, GenPA requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks (99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus) and real-world manipulation tasks. Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk on a single H100 GPU, achieving 1.7-3.4x speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines. Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of visual generation backbones for efficient robot control. Ablations across visual tasks and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe.

AI.tldr: Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks (99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus) an...

title: Participant-Independent Validation of Smartphone Video and Wearable Inertial Sensing for Coach-Rated Running-Form Classification
summary: Participant-Independent Validation of Smartphone Video and Wearable Inertial Sensing for Coach-Rated Running-Form Classification 10 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables Automated running-form assessment could make technique feedback more accessible outside professional coaching and laboratory settings. We evaluated a low-cost pipeline combining side-view smartphone video with wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) acceleration for coach-rated running-form classification. The dataset comprised 294 labeled recordings from 20 runners and 1,555 windows across four cues: landing position, suspension, triple extension, and upper-body posture. The primary analysis used 100 repeated four-runner holdout splits, recording-level aggregation of window predictions, and LightGBM models with hyperparameters fixed from prior modality-specific searches. Video-only LightGBM achieved mean macro F1 of 0.310, versus 0.168 for a majority-class baseline. Adding IMU features reduced macro F1 to 0.267, a paired mean difference of -0.043. Robustness analysis with Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM found that video-only models had higher mean performance than the majority baseline, whereas fusion effects depended on model family: Linear SVM showed a small positive effect, Logistic Regression was approximately neutral, and tree-based models showed lower performance with fusion. These results indicate a modest participant-independent signal in smartphone pose features. However, apparent IMU-fusion gains depended strongly on validation design, model family, and target category. The gap between recording-level and participant-independent performance underscores the need for runner-holdout evaluation and suggests that simple feature-level fusion does not reliably generalize to unseen runners.

AI.tldr: Video-only LightGBM achieved mean macro F1 of 0.310, versus 0.168 for a majority-class baseline.

title: Social-Qwen: From Individual Nonverbal Cues and Emotion to Multiparty Social Dynamics Understanding with Instruction Tuning
summary: Social-Qwen: From Individual Nonverbal Cues and Emotion to Multiparty Social Dynamics Understanding with Instruction Tuning Effective participation in multiparty scenarios requires robots to move beyond individual toward understanding group-level social dynamics, which are inherently complex due to the interplay of nonverbal cues, internal states, and interaction context. Existing approaches often rely on end-to-end deterministic models, while recent state-of-the-art methods such as large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) address this issue to some extent but remain limited by their size and computational cost for real-time applications. Moreover, both approaches are constrained by the scarcity of multiparty interaction data and annotations, which describe how individual nonverbal cues and emotional states contribute to social dynamics which describe collective outcomes such as group engagement. We hypothesize that explicitly modeling individual-level states is essential for accurate group-level understanding. To this end, we present Social-Qwen, a two-stage framework that first analyzes each participant's nonverbal cues and emotions, then infers group-level engagement using instruction-tuned representations. To mitigate the lack of individual annotations in group datasets, we employ knowledge distillation to transfer supervision signals. Experiments on the OUC-CGE dataset show that Social-Qwen significantly outperforms prior end-to-end baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance in group engagement analysis, demonstrating the promise of instruction tuning for scalable social intelligence in robots. We further evaluate robustness by testing generalization to (1) an in-house dataset spanning multiple social activities and (2) estimating other social dynamics such as group harmony. Results suggest consistent performance, highlighting Social-Qwen as a promising approach toward real-time social intelligence for intelligent agents.

AI.tldr: Existing approaches often rely on end-to-end deterministic models, while recent state-of-the-art methods such as large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) address this issue to some extent but remain limited by their size a...

title: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time
summary: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.

AI.tldr: Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-...

title: Prediction-Powered Regression via Calibration: Beyond the Supervised Minimax Benchmark
summary: Prediction-Powered Regression via Calibration: Beyond the Supervised Minimax Benchmark We study nonparametric regression with limited labeled data and abundant observations carrying potentially inaccurate pseudo-labels. Our proposed method, weighted prediction-powered regression via calibration (wPPRC), first calibrates pseudo-labels using labeled data, then fits a predictor by weighted regression using observed and calibrated responses. Over Hölder classes, we derive nonasymptotic excess-risk bounds for clipped ReLU estimators and establish a minimax lower bound for the corresponding regression problem. Under suitable conditions, the upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors. Moreover, wPPRC can achieve a worst-case risk of smaller order than the minimax risks under four baseline observation structures on the same joint distribution class, demonstrating the value of additional pseudo-labels. We also construct a validation-selected (VS) estimator using an independent labeled validation sample to choose the weight. The VS estimator satisfies an expected-risk oracle inequality and preserves the improvement over the baseline minimax risks with the same total labeled-data budget. Simulations and an application to predicting homeless counts illustrate the gains of the proposed estimators.

AI.tldr: Our proposed method, weighted prediction-powered regression via calibration (wPPRC), first calibrates pseudo-labels using labeled data, then fits a predictor by weighted regression using observed and calibrated respon...

title: Lorentz symmetry in self-supervised representation learning
summary: Lorentz symmetry in self-supervised representation learning 9 pages, 5 figures Self-supervised learning (SSL) and explicit physical inductive biases have driven major advances in jet tagging, yet they are typically pursued along separate tracks. In this work, we unify both paradigms by integrating the Lorentz-equivariant Geometric Algebra Transformer slim (L-GATr-slim) architecture with the LeJEPA framework for representation learning. Pre-training on 100 million jets from the JetClass dataset, we optimize towards a latent space, which is invariant across physics-motivated jet augmentations. We demonstrate that enforcing Lorentz symmetry in the latent space is critical for representation quality and that this can be achieved either architecturally or learned via kinematic augmentations. With a standard non-invariant Transformer backbone, LeJEPA outperforms established autoregressive, masked particle modelling, and self-distillation baselines in linear- and MLP-probe accuracy, with L-GATr-slim providing further complementary gains. Across downstream benchmarks, our pre-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained from scratch or through different pre-training objectives.

AI.tldr: We demonstrate that enforcing Lorentz symmetry in the latent space is critical for representation quality and that this can be achieved either architecturally or learned via kinematic augmentations.

title: Demographic Encoding is Not Exposure: Fairness and Privacy in Chest X-ray Foundation Models
summary: Demographic Encoding is Not Exposure: Fairness and Privacy in Chest X-ray Foundation Models Medical foundation models encode patient demographics and can reveal whether a patient was in the training set, and these properties are often treated as one problem. We tested whether they are aligned by measuring demographic encoding, diagnostic fairness gaps and membership-inference vulnerability on the same models. We trained 200 linear or multilayer-perceptron (MLP) heads on frozen BiomedCLIP, DINOv2 and RAD-DINO embeddings, with three seeds, and audited them on CheXpert and NIH ChestX-ray14. Demographic encoding explained almost no variance in patient vulnerability, and all 72 CheXpert associations were statistically equivalent to zero. Erasing linearly decodable demographics left leakage unchanged but reduced age-related underdiagnosis gaps. Leakage depended instead on head capacity and training length. On RAD-DINO, a linear head reached a membership-inference area under the curve (AUC) of 0.694, compared with 0.907 for a 30-epoch MLP, at similar test performance. Fairness and privacy should therefore be audited separately, and linear heads or shorter training reduce leakage with little or no loss of utility. The code is available on GitHub for public use.

AI.tldr: We trained 200 linear or multilayer-perceptron (MLP) heads on frozen BiomedCLIP, DINOv2 and RAD-DINO embeddings, with three seeds, and audited them on CheXpert and NIH ChestX-ray14.

title: A Comparison of Uncertainty in AI and Dynamical Climate Ensembles
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables; supplementary information included
summary: A Comparison of Uncertainty in AI and Dynamical Climate Ensembles 26 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables; supplementary information included Climate model ensembles and their uncertainty estimates are essential for evaluating risk and designing climate policy. Yet, in the assessment of newly developed AI climate models, evaluating uncertainty is often secondary to diagnosing mean-state climate biases and trends. In this work, we conduct the first systematic comparison of uncertainty representation in ensembles of state-of-the-art AI and dynamical atmospheric climate models. Examining 2-meter temperature, 500 hPa geopotential height, and precipitable water, we find that the AI ensemble exhibits reduced internal variability and model uncertainty across variables relative to the dynamical ensemble. We show that this dampened variability causes the AI ensemble to produce more limited climate extremes and yields underdispersion relative to ERA5. Under a uniform warming scenario, the AI ensemble shows increased model uncertainty. Dynamical models grapple with their own challenges, exhibiting stronger miscalibration (overdispersion) relative to ERA5 and larger climate biases than the AI models. As AI and dynamical climate models are mutually integrated into operational climate prediction, careful consideration of their differences in uncertainty representations is crucial for grounded assessment of climate risk.

AI.tldr: Yet, in the assessment of newly developed AI climate models, evaluating uncertainty is often secondary to diagnosing mean-state climate biases and trends.

title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals
summary: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.

AI.tldr: Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the stat...

title: Data-Driven Identification of Uncertainty Sets with Conformance Guarantees
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to IEEE
summary: Data-Driven Identification of Uncertainty Sets with Conformance Guarantees 16 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to IEEE Formal verification and controller synthesis require accurate models. Conformance relations specify the required accuracy of a model such that properties established for the model carry over to the target system. Existing methods for establishing them from measured data are typically restricted to a single relation, a specific model class, or a downstream verification algorithm. We present ConfID, a unified framework that establishes reachset, trace, and simulation conformance with respect to measured traces by identifying uncertainty sets for a given, possibly nonlinear nominal model. Unmodeled effects are thus captured by nondeterminism rather than by refining the nominal dynamics. For all three conformance relations, the identification is a linear program that minimizes the size of the reachable sets; only its constraints depend on the relation. We further derive distribution-free bounds on the probability that the identified models are conformant for unseen behaviors. Experiments on simulated and real-world data evaluate the models identified for the three relations, confirm the guarantees, and show that these models cover unseen behaviors more reliably than baselines, with comparable or smaller sets.

AI.tldr: Existing methods for establishing them from measured data are typically restricted to a single relation, a specific model class, or a downstream verification algorithm.

title: Optimal Regret Lower Bounds in Matrix Games
summary: Optimal Regret Lower Bounds in Matrix Games 22 pages, 2 figures We study learning in two-player zero-sum games, also known as matrix games, in which two players with $m$ and $n$ actions repeatedly select mixed strategies for $T$ rounds. The learning dynamics based on optimistic Hedge guarantee regrets of $O(\log(mn))$, which improve to $O(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$ if each player knows the number of actions of the opponent, whereas matching regret lower bounds have been known only for specific learning dynamics. We prove that, for every deterministic learning dynamic, there exists a payoff matrix for which the maximum individual regret is $\Omega(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$ for a wide range of $m$ and $n$. Together with the upper bound $O(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$, this lower bound shows that the minimax regret of deterministic learning dynamics in matrix games is $\Theta(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$ in this regime. For all $m$, $n$, and $T$, we also prove the lower bound $\Omega(\min\{T,\log\min\{m,n\}\})$. These lower bounds hold even if each player also observes the strategies and the feedback of the opponent. Our main technical contribution is an adaptive construction of the payoff matrix. While running the algorithms of the two players, we add in each round a rank-one matrix that keeps the feedback of the previous rounds unchanged and increases a lower bound on the sum of the regrets of the two players. As by-products, we obtain lower bounds on the rate at which the average strategies converge to a Nash equilibrium and on the query complexity of matrix-vector products that deterministic algorithms need to compute an approximate Nash equilibrium.

AI.tldr: Optimal Regret Lower Bounds in Matrix Games 22 pages, 2 figures We study learning in two-player zero-sum games, also known as matrix games, in which two players with $m$ and $n$ actions repeatedly select mixed strateg...

title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
summary: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates 15 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

AI.tldr: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates 15 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party pack...

title: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search
summary: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search 13 pages, 8 figures In measurement-based quantum computation and quantum repeater networks, graph-structured quantum states called graph states play a central role as an essential resource. In a graph state, each vertex corresponds to a qubit, and each edge is prepared by applying one controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Local complementation, which toggles adjacencies among the neighbors of a selected vertex, produces operationally equivalent graph states up to an inexpensive operation called local Clifford gates. Therefore, finding equivalent graphs up to local complementation with fewer edges and lower maximum degree can reduce the preparation cost, such as the number of CZ gates and the circuit depth. In this paper, we formulate the problem of finding a desirable equivalent graph via local complementations as a state space search problem. We apply a heuristic search algorithm, greedy best-first search (GBFS), to the formulated problem. Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most of the graphs constructed from quantum LDPC codes. In addition, we empirically analyze GBFS's search behavior, confirming that we need search rather than stopping at the first local minimum to find the best solution.

AI.tldr: Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-d...

title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance
summary: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.

AI.tldr: Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity.

title: SignalCount: Approximate Counts with Structured and Semantic Predicates in Seconds
summary: SignalCount: Approximate Counts with Structured and Semantic Predicates in Seconds 12 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables Many applications store records with structured columns and a text document, and ask how many records in a filtered set meet a criterion that only a reader of the text can judge, such as "How many patients with type 2 diabetes, aged 40 to 70, stopped metformin because their blood sugar stayed high?" An interactive application needs this count in seconds, as the user types the criterion, to decide whether the matching set is worth materializing with a batch pipeline in which an LLM judges the records. Prior approximate query processing over such semantic predicates has an expensive model, the oracle, label a sample at query time, so every query waits for the oracle. We present SignalCount, a production system that answers COUNT queries with structured and semantic predicates and calls no oracle at query time, even for ad-hoc criteria. Its oracle is the production LLM judge, and the judge's logged verdicts calibrate, offline, the fast classifier that already runs in front of the judge. At query time, SignalCount counts the filtered set exactly and draws a uniform sample of at most 1,000 records in one columnar scan, scores the sample with the classifier, and multiplies the average calibrated probability by the exact count. Its 90% interval combines a sampling term with one-sided, rate-dependent margins for calibration error, fitted by split conformal prediction across tenants. In a multi-tenant production deployment, latency has a p99 of 3.8 s and stays flat as the filtered set grows beyond the sample. On tenants held out from fitting, the interval covers the count that the production pipeline returns in 92% of estimates, although estimates run about 15% high in aggregate, because a calibration nearly unbiased per record is still biased per criterion.

AI.tldr: SignalCount: Approximate Counts with Structured and Semantic Predicates in Seconds 12 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables Many applications store records with structured columns and a text document, and ask how many records in...

title: How Systems Treat Intent: A Faceted Taxonomy of Intent for Human-AI Co-Creation
summary: How Systems Treat Intent: A Faceted Taxonomy of Intent for Human-AI Co-Creation Human-AI interaction depends on systems acting on user intent rather than explicit procedures, even when that intent is incomplete, evolving, or partially communicable. Literature organizing systems by interaction technique, workflow stage, or division of labor, offer limited insight into which facet of intent an interaction mechanism addresses. We introduce a six-facet taxonomy of intent, grounded in philosophical accounts of mind, action, and meaning, and apply it to systems presented in 198 papers from eleven SIGCHI venues. Our analysis reveals that different forms of incomplete intent are associated with distinct interaction and authorship strategies, showing that mechanisms that appear similar often address fundamentally different intent-related problems. This exposes blind spots, as intent is rarely represented as an interaction object, authorship provenance is rarely tracked, and tentative preferences are rarely distinguished from firm commitments. The taxonomy offers a lens for analyzing and designing AI systems around the facets of intent they address.

AI.tldr: We introduce a six-facet taxonomy of intent, grounded in philosophical accounts of mind, action, and meaning, and apply it to systems presented in 198 papers from eleven SIGCHI venues.

title: Random Feature Neural Networks for Stochastic Optimal Control
summary: Random Feature Neural Networks for Stochastic Optimal Control Random feature neural networks (RFNNs) sample their hidden parameters once and train only the output layer. We analyze RFNNs as feedback policies for finite-horizon stochastic control with trajectory-dependent objectives. A policy change alters later states, so the error that matters is the objective error of the induced trajectory rather than a pointwise regression error. We extend the quantitative random-feature approximation theory for PDE solutions and nonlinear regression to feedback control. We investigate the objective error of an RFNN policy through two sources, approximation of the policy by random features and estimation of the objective from finitely many paths. A stability estimate for the controlled trajectory turns a policy error into an objective error. Under bounded actions, a regular benchmark policy and exact empirical minimization, the expected objective gap to the benchmark policy is at most of order $N^{-1/2}+\sqrt{N(1+\log N)/n}$, with $N$ the feature width per output coordinate and $n$ the number of paths. At fixed sample size the two terms trade off in $N$, and balancing them gives $N\asymp\sqrt{n/\log n}$. Across a wide range of examples, estimated gaps generally decrease with width and sample size, and RFNNs show an advantage when simulated paths are limited. We also study Parsimonious Random Feature Learning (PRFL), which grows and prunes the random dictionary during training while training only the output coefficients. At matched retained width and training budget, PRFL improves on a fixed RFNN in the LQ and Heston comparisons, while the fully trained network remains best in those examples.

AI.tldr: Under bounded actions, a regular benchmark policy and exact empirical minimization, the expected objective gap to the benchmark policy is at most of order $N^{-1/2}+\sqrt{N(1+\log N)/n}$, with $N$ the feature width pe...

title: Semantic-aware Decoding for Diverse Text-to-SQL under Schema Ambiguity
summary: Semantic-aware Decoding for Diverse Text-to-SQL under Schema Ambiguity Real-world text-to-SQL systems often face schema ambiguity, where a question can map to multiple plausible schema elements. To support downstream disambiguation, SQL generation systems should include diverse interpretations among their top-k predictions. However, large language models (LLMs) typically favor a single interpretation, producing highly skewed outputs. We propose Semantic-aware Logit Adjustment (SLA), a training-free decoding method that promotes diverse SQL generation by adjusting token logits based on semantic similarity between schema elements. Unlike prior approaches that rely on reasoning-intensive prompting or task-specific fine-tuning, SLA is efficient, model-agnostic, and easy to deploy. Experiments show that SLA consistently improves interpretation coverage over standard decoding and remains competitive with existing diversity-oriented methods at substantially lower inference cost.

AI.tldr: We propose Semantic-aware Logit Adjustment (SLA), a training-free decoding method that promotes diverse SQL generation by adjusting token logits based on semantic similarity between schema elements.

title: Constellations of Colour: Mapping Semantic Neighbourhoods in CLIP
comment: In Proceedings of Explainable AI for the Arts Workshop 2026 (XAIxArts 2026) arXiv:2607.20131
summary: Constellations of Colour: Mapping Semantic Neighbourhoods in CLIP In Proceedings of Explainable AI for the Arts Workshop 2026 (XAIxArts 2026) How do vision-language models organise the cultural and perceptual dimensions of colour language? This pictorial presents a research-through-design visualisation of colour semantics in CLIP, a pretrained vision-language model. A dataset of 2,500 named colours is embedded with CLIP's text encoder, projected to a 2D map, and connected via a thresholded minimum spanning tree to create disjoint "constellations" of related colour terms. The resulting maps offer a model for navigating the semantic and perceptual relationships between colour terms. The visualisations reveal gradients along familiar axes (hue, lightness, chroma), as well as semantic neighbourhoods, including botanical language (hyacinth, cornflower, tulip), fictional references ("Robin Hood green", "warlock purple"), and food (butterscotch, toast, toffee). These visualisations give designers and creatives a map for exploring colour linguistically and building palettes by semantic association, pointing towards interpretable, artist-facing colour tools derived from foundation models.

title: Psychological State Monitoring Methods Based on Multimodal Emotion Recognition
summary: Psychological State Monitoring Methods Based on Multimodal Emotion Recognition 8 pages, 4 figures The computer-Based Multimodal Emotion Recognition System needs to increase the accuracy and reliability of psychological state monitoring. A hierarchical framework was proposed in this paper to integrate facial images, speech signals and other physiological indicators of emotion in time and space for more complete analysis of human emotions. Synchronously sample data streams from webcams, microphones and wearable sensors, and then preprocess and extract features specific to each type of data. A high-end fusion architecture is adopted to combine early- and late-fusion methods and thus robustly integrate cross-modal information. The overall recognition accuracy and mean F1-score of the fused multimodal system are both about 91% and 0.88, respectively, which are superior to the best unimodal approach (face, 88% accuracy and F1-score 0.88). title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
summary: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.

title: Temporal Persistence for Stylized Rendering: Historical Image Storage and Reconstruction
summary: Temporal Persistence for Stylized Rendering: Historical Image Storage and Reconstruction 19 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables The overlapping silhouettes and gradual fading in The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask (released April 27, 2000) produce a distinctive depiction of motion blur, in which earlier scene states remain visible as part of the current image. Reproducing this appearance in a modern renderer involves decisions about when historical images are sampled, how their contributions are retained, and how the resulting history can be represented within the available memory and processing budget. In this paper, we investigate these decisions through complete image histories, shared image regions, and selectively retained pixel changes, using Godot engine implementations evaluated against independently composited references. For a ten-image history sampled at 20 Hz on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti, half-float storage halves history allocation and reduces median storage-pass duration by factors of 2.40 at 720p and 1.73 at 1080p, preserving the supplied source precision. The adaptive experiments examine how memory savings depend on reconstruction metadata and allocation, including a sparse representation that reduces allocation by 83.81% at low resolution with 445.25 times the GPU duration.

title: Which Vertebral Landmark Errors Change a Cobb Angle? Geometry-Weighted Supervision for Radiographic Landmark Regression
summary: Which Vertebral Landmark Errors Change a Cobb Angle? Geometry-Weighted Supervision for Radiographic Landmark Regression 13 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables A network that localizes vertebral corners can reduce pixel error while rotating the line used to measure spinal curvature. We derive a training loss from the geometry of a three-angle reader. Of the eight corner-displacement degrees of freedom of a vertebral quadrilateral, one local direction rotates its left-to-right chord. The angular sensitivity in this direction is inversely proportional to chord width. An orthonormal Hadamard basis lets us give this residual extra weight during training while retaining supervision on the other seven directions. In five-fold image-level development experiments on 372 anteroposterior radiographs, we compared three objectives across 45 fits of the same landmark network. The three-seed corner ensemble reduced pooled symmetric percentage error from 18.45% with coordinate supervision to 17.20% with geometry weighting. Adding a soft pairwise-angle term yielded 16.89%, a paired difference of $-1.56$ percentage points from coordinate supervision (95% image-bootstrap interval $[-2.51,-0.61]$). The interval for the increment from adding the soft term included zero. In a single-fold comparison, direct unit-chord supervision also reduced error, and its difference from geometry weighting was uncertain. Across single-seed runs, rotational residual error fell by 36.1% while normalized corner error rose from 2.60% to 2.71%. Perturbing one vertebra at a time also showed when a small rotation changes the selected end pair. These results identify a measurable trade-off between landmark fidelity and agreement with a specified geometric reader. The evaluation concerns an internal image-level split and landmark-derived target angles.

AI.tldr: In five-fold image-level development experiments on 372 anteroposterior radiographs, we compared three objectives across 45 fits of the same landmark network.

title: Duplicate- and Patient-Overlap Leakage in Brain MRI Tumor Classification: A Multi-Model Evaluation
summary: Duplicate- and Patient-Overlap Leakage in Brain MRI Tumor Classification: A Multi-Model Evaluation 14 pages, 6 figures, 2 table Background. Repeated MRI images and distinct slices from the same patient can both compromise evaluation of brain tumor classifiers. Objective. We audited image duplication and examined how patient overlap relates to discrimination, probability error and model ranking. Methods. The Cheng/Figshare dataset contains 3,064 contrast-enhanced T1 MRI slices, three tumor classes and 233 recorded patient IDs. The dataset author advised treating the IDs as individuals, but original DICOM records were unavailable for verification. Four CNN architectures were trained under image-level and recorded-ID-disjoint protocols with five folds matched on size and class counts (40 original runs). A patient-cluster bootstrap quantified uncertainty. The extension added 60 split-seed runs, 40 training-seed runs and 72 fixed-test sibling-exposure runs with class-matched other-patient controls. Results. We found no exact duplicate images and little evidence of cross-patient near-duplicates among screened pairs. Image-level minus recorded-ID-disjoint balanced accuracy ranged from +0.0318 to +0.0462 across models. Expected calibration error and multiclass Brier scores were lower on the image-level evaluation sample. The balanced-accuracy difference persisted across new seeds for ResNet50 and DenseNet121, but their original ranking reversal did not replicate. Only ResNet50 in fold 2 passed Holm correction in the five-test exposure family. All 16 correlated exploratory subgroup estimates were positive, with no consistent dose-response. Conclusions. Patient overlap was associated with higher apparent performance on this benchmark. Fixed-test comparisons could not isolate patient identity from shared anatomy or acquisition characteristics. No independent external clinical validation was performed.

AI.tldr: Duplicate- and Patient-Overlap Leakage in Brain MRI Tumor Classification: A Multi-Model Evaluation 14 pages, 6 figures, 2 table Background.

title: Quality-Control Policies Shape Model Behaviour in Computational Pathology
comment: 50 pages, 7 main figures, 22 supplementary figures, 1 table; includes supplementary methods and results, and 5 ancillary data files
summary: Quality-Control Policies Shape Model Behaviour in Computational Pathology 50 pages, 7 main figures, 22 supplementary figures, 1 table; includes supplementary methods and results, and 5 ancillary data files Quality-control policies determine which image regions are used by computational pathology models, but their effects are difficult to isolate when quality estimation and input selection are coupled. We make these policies explicit, configurable and testable. We introduce PathQC-3C, comprising 1,661 densely annotated regions from 1,194 haematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images across 32 cancer/tissue categories, and TileNet, a framework that separates dense tissue/background/artefact estimation from task-specific input-selection policies. We evaluated the default predictor across three held-out cohorts and against harmonised quality-control comparators, assessed policy decisions in a blinded single-pathologist audit, and tested alternative policies in three downstream settings. In retrospective CAMELYON16 multiple-instance learning, background-aware selection improved the pooled out-of-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.758 to 0.839 compared with random sampling from the same exhaustive candidate pool under a fixed tile budget. In weak-label lung classification, strict artefact exclusion reduced the pre-matching candidate pool by approximately 43%, with small metric-dependent differences after matching training-set size and patient contribution. PathQCAug, which composites real artefact components during tumour-stroma model adaptation, improved macro Dice on high-artefact tiles under severe held-out composited artefacts across three training seeds and outperformed random-erasing and clean-tissue controls. Separating quality estimation from policy execution provides an auditable way to control which image content enters computational pathology models; the appropriate policy is task specific, and clinical utility remains to be established.

title: Beyond Outlier Rejection: Transient-Aware Reconstruction of Multi-Stack MRI
summary: Beyond Outlier Rejection: Transient-Aware Reconstruction of Multi-Stack MRI 11 pages, 6 Figures Clinical MRI typically acquires the organ of interest as consecutive stacks of 2D slices in different orientations. Reconstruction methods such as SVRTK and NeSVoR fuse them into one volume and down-weight what does not fit, although in living tissue the change during the scan is often the signal itself and can contain clinically relevant physiological information, such as fetal motion and uterine contraction. We propose an analysis-by-synthesis decomposition that explains every acquired voxel through its exact acquisition geometry as a static anatomy shared by all stacks, a rigid and smooth non-rigid motion per stack, and a sparse transient field per stack for changes during one acquisition only. A robust reweighting keeps such changes out of the anatomy. The model is fitted per subject without training data, with one configuration for all datasets. On a digital phantom with known ground truth, static changes are kept entirely in the anatomy, and the transient field of the stack that saw a transient recovers 68% of it at 12mm radius. From identical inputs, the anatomy predicts held-out stacks better than SVRTK and NeSVoR on uterine (NCC 0.897 against 0.874 and 0.863, 123 patients) and on prostate MRI from unseen sites and scanners (0.847 against 0.795 and 0.757, 85 patients), and on fetal brain MRI as well as SVRTK and better than NeSVoR (0.771 against 0.763 and 0.747, 83 fetuses). The transient fields flag corrupted fetal slices with an AUROC of 0.94 against expert raters. As the input of a frozen anomaly detector trained on healthy subjects only, the anatomy localizes radiologist-delineated uterine lesions better than the SVRTK and NeSVoR volumes (AUROC 0.76 against 0.71 and 0.71, 37 patients).

AI.tldr: Beyond Outlier Rejection: Transient-Aware Reconstruction of Multi-Stack MRI 11 pages, 6 Figures Clinical MRI typically acquires the organ of interest as consecutive stacks of 2D slices in different orientations.

title: Flood forecasting using a physics-guided conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model
comment: 47 pages, 25 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Journal of Hydrology
summary: Flood forecasting using a physics-guided conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model 47 pages, 25 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Journal of Hydrology High-resolution flood forecasting with full two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers remains computationally expensive, even on GPUs. We develop a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that forecasts the evolution of 30 m water-depth fields over a four-day horizon for the Des Plaines River watershed, Illinois. The model is trained on SynxFlow SWE simulations of 113 historical storms observed across twelve Midwestern states (2003-2024), each under three antecedent-wetness scenarios, and can optionally be conditioned on coarse 100 m or 150 m hydrodynamic simulations. Because reverse diffusion is stochastic, every forecast is a 20-member ensemble drawn from the same trained model. Coarse conditioning reduces the four-day mean water-depth RMSE of the ensemble mean from 0.170 m to 0.054 m (100 m) and 0.048 m (150 m). The coarser 150 m conditioning also gives the best critical success index (0.839), false alarm ratio, CRPS and Brier score at lower cost, so finer conditioning does not guarantee better skill. Averaging members reduces error by 5-11% relative to a single realization, and the ensemble provides spatially explicit exceedance probabilities, although the ensembles are under-dispersive (spread-to-error ratios 0.35-0.73). On a single GPU, a four-day forecast over 26 non-overlapping patches is 7.8x, 11.0x and 16.3x faster than the 30 m simulation for the 100 m, 150 m and unconditioned configurations, and projected speedups for a 14-day forecast reach 12-49x for one member and 48-58x for 20 members. Physics-guided diffusion models are thus promising probabilistic surrogates for regional-scale flood forecasting.

AI.tldr: We develop a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that forecasts the evolution of 30 m water-depth fields over a four-day horizon for the Des Plaines River watershed, Illinois.

title: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models
summary: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models Pending review with ARR Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokmål, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at .

title: Vetoes and missed agreements in language-model bargaining
summary: Vetoes and missed agreements in language-model bargaining 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables A language model played three representatives, each instructed to get the best payoff for its own group. One representative requested a plan, another chose the sole offer, and all three voted. If anyone voted no, each group received its fallback payoff. In 60 games with Qwen3-Next-80B, the representative at risk of a loss always requested a plan that would leave everyone better off. In each game, two copies of the proposer saw the same payoffs, peer request and reminder that the offer needed three yes votes. Showing the proposer how many groups gained under each plan raised mutually beneficial agreements from 6/60 to 31/60 (paired increase 41.7 percentage points, conservative 95% interval 18.8 to 58.5). Two of the four plans benefited everyone, so picking uniformly would put a mutual gain on the ballot half the time on average. In an earlier study, GPT-4.1 played 12 conflict games under two message conditions. Majority rule passed 15 of 24 offers, all at one group's expense. Unanimity passed two, both mutual gains. In the Qwen games, voters never saw the counts. They approved all 37 offers that helped everyone. On all 83 offers that would have cost one group points, its representative voted no.

AI.tldr: Vetoes and missed agreements in language-model bargaining 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables A language model played three representatives, each instructed to get the best payoff for its own group.

title: The AMPEL Platform: An Open-Source Project for Developing Hospital-Wide Clinical Decision Support Systems under EU-Regulation
summary: The AMPEL Platform: An Open-Source Project for Developing Hospital-Wide Clinical Decision Support Systems under EU-Regulation 15 pages, 5 figures As incentives to digitize more and more aspects of medical healthcare are gaining traction, additional medical data is becoming available. A major goal is to use this data to gain further insights, support medical staff, and ultimately improve patient care. This demands sophisticated solutions that can handle current and future vast amounts of data, all without disrupting well-established workflows of care takers. Additionally, the solution must fulfill the documentation and risk-management obligations of the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), which governs whether a device may be used in patient care in Europe. In this context, we introduce the AMPEL platform, an open-source solution for creating clinical decision support systems (CDSS) that fulfil the requirements of the MDR. Centered around a message broker (Kafka), it adopts an event-driven, distributed architecture, allowing for scaling and efficient processing of medical data as it gets generated. Relying on platform-specific events to implicitly describe the platform's interfaces makes it both extensible and agnostic to the hospital information system in use. With these events being defined in the Protocol Buffers format, medically evaluated algorithms can be independently implemented in a variety of programming languages and easily linked to the platform, extending its analytic capabilities as desired. The platform features a basic UI and alert functionality that can be used to gain medical staff's attention and present analysis results in a traceable and explainable fashion. We further show in a use case how the platform was used to build LAMPE, a CDSS developed and operated at University of Leipzig Medical Center. It demonstrates how the platform solution can be used in a complex and already established environment, while acknowledging current limitations and outlining planned developments to overcome these.

title: EID-Net: Endoscopic Illumination-aware Degradation Correction Network
summary: EID-Net: Endoscopic Illumination-aware Degradation Correction Network 7 pages, 5 figures Endoscopic images captured under complex illumination conditions often suffer from spatially non-uniform exposure degradation, including local under-exposure, over-exposure, and illumination-induced color variation. These degradations are usually entangled with tissue structures, making it challenging for general-purpose low-light enhancement and image restoration methods to improve visibility while preserving local structural and chromatic cues. In this paper, we propose EID-Net, an endoscopic illumination-aware degradation correction network for structure-preserving endoscopic illumination correction. Rather than treating illumination correction as a global intensity adjustment, EID-Net explicitly extracts an endoscopy-oriented degradation prior from the input image to characterize illumination-related variations in a unified representation. This prior is then introduced into the decoder through an illumination-modulated transposed attention mechanism, where it adaptively guides feature aggregation by modulating the key-value feature subspace. Extensive experiments on CEC, Endo4IE, EndoVis17, and EndoVis18 datasets demonstrate that EID-Net performs favorably against recent endoscopic enhancement and general image restoration methods. The code is available at .

title: Reducing Permutation Sensitivity in Multimodal Large Language Models via Shared Positions and Attention-Only Distillation
summary: Reducing Permutation Sensitivity in Multimodal Large Language Models via Shared Positions and Attention-Only Distillation In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on improving permutation robustness while preserving accuracy. First, we categorize permutation bias phenomena into four representative scenarios. Then, we take the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) dataset as an example under text-option reordering scenario to analyze the root cause of permutation bias. Based on this root cause analysis and set encoding strategy, we investigate shared positions with blocked cross-unit attention (SP-B) and extend this design to bidirectional cross-unit attention (SP-V) for modality exchange. However, these structural changes may reduce predictive accuracy. To recover model capability across different scenarios under the SP structure, an attention-only distillation from frozen native models is proposed. Shared positions reduce permutation sensitivity, and attention-only distillation improves accuracy under the shared-position structure. Across all three models, our method is comparable to or better than majority voting in macro-average all-permutation accuracy, and outperforms supervised fine-tuning by 1.95-4.20 percentage points. This work provides valuable insight into permutation bias mitigation and model capability recovery.

AI.tldr: Across all three models, our method is comparable to or better than majority voting in macro-average all-permutation accuracy, and outperforms supervised fine-tuning by 1.95-4.20 percentage points.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Soft-Constrained AC-OPF in Multiphase Distribution Systems
summary: Self-Supervised Learning for Soft-Constrained AC-OPF in Multiphase Distribution Systems Code: This paper presents a self-supervised learning framework for fast, soft-constrained AC optimal power flow (OPF) in unbalanced multiphase distribution systems. The soft AC-OPF objective balances operating cost, renewable energy curtailment, and penalties for violating operating limits. A neural network predicts distributed energy resource (DER) setpoints conditioned on operating conditions, switch configurations, and objective weights. The predicted setpoints are then processed through a DER projection and differentiable AC power flow to enforce device limits and network equalities. The framework is trained by directly minimizing the AC-OPF objective, without optimal-solution labels. Experiments on 123-, 240-, and 906-bus systems yield mean objective gaps of 0.32%, 0.92%, and 0.56%, respectively, relative to IPOPT, across wide operating ranges. Across these systems and the evaluated high-load/low-generation and low-load/high-generation scenarios, the largest mean gap is 1.04%, with mean speedups of 58-5272 times relative to IPOPT.
